 Flood of new evidence? Ancient wood discovery fuels fresh Noah’s Ark speculation
 The millennia-old search for Noah’s Ark may be heating up as archaeologists revealed wood fragments buried about 9 metres beneath the slope of Mount Ararat in Turkey.  
 Christian Li Volsi Digital Reporter 3 min read November 11, 2026 - 8:20PM Researchers investigating the Durupinar Formation near Mount Ararat have recently announced that pieces of wood were found about 9 metres (30 feet) below the surface of the mountain’s slope.  
 The uncovered wood fragment appears to be a blackened, cracked specimen with man-made marks reportedly consistent with ancient tool work.
 Sivas Cumhuriyet University archaeologist Dr Cenker Atila said the wooden fragments found at the depth could belong to an ancient period.
 The millennia-old search for Noah’s Ark may be heating up as archaeologists revealed wood fragments buried about 9 metres beneath the slope of Mount Ararat in Turkey. Picture: Facebook, Noah's Ark Scans "The wood was discovered approximately 9 meters below the surface on the southern slope of the formation,” Dr Atila said.
 “One of the wooden pieces clearly shows signs of human workmanship. Its surface appears to have been slightly shaped and flattened using an axe or a knife.
 “The fact that these wooden fragments were found at such a considerable depth indicates that they may belong to an ancient period."
 The fragment has been sent for testing at four laboratories in different countries to determine the species and whether it shows traces of tree sap or pitch, a dark, waterproof substance made from tar.
 The laboratories are located in Turkey, Switzerland, the United States, and France.
 They are also analysing soil and core samples and conducting carbon-14 dating.
 The Durupinar Formation was identified in 1959 by Turkish army captain Ilhan Durupinar, who noticed its boat-shaped outline. Picture: Facebook, Noah's Ark Scans Dr Atila said recent rain and a landslide led to his discovery and expressed excitement about the significance of the find.
 “It was very exciting that many archaeologists and local villagers know that after heavy rain, landslides can occur on the slope area, and after that, many archaeological objects can appear on the surface,” he added.
 “I was already walking around the site every day, looking for evidence. One day after the heavy rain, I noticed some black marks on the hillside; then I carefully removed a little soil from that area, and I found some wooden pieces like this.
 “It was incredibly exciting for me; I shouted with joy, ‘I think I found a piece of Noah’s Ark!’
 “This piece is very important … maybe there is a human-made sign here.”
 The formation has long been believed to be connected to Noah’s Ark, with researchers outlining that the approximately 157-metre length corresponds to the vessel described in Genesis.
 An image of the Durupinar Formation in 1961 shows the mysterious outline. Picture: Facebook, Noah's Ark Scans By biblical measurements, the ark would have been about 157 metres long, 26 metres wide, and 16 metres tall.
 However, one caveat remains: according to the Bible, Noah was instructed to coat the ark, inside and out, with pitch.
 Despite the wood’s charred appearance, the photographs do not prove that fragments came from an ancient vessel, nor do they prove a tar-like pitch composite was present.
 The discovery follows a 2019 radar survey by US defence scientist Dr Khosrow Bakhtar, which revealed straight lines and angular patterns beneath the Durupinar Formation, which researchers interpreted as possible wall-like structures with passageways and compartments.
 Radar readings show how signals respond to different underground materials and boundaries, but physical examination is still needed to identify exactly what was detected.
 A radar scan conducted on the Durupinar Formation revealed non-geological features, including organised hallways and tunnelling, according to researchers. Picture: Facebook, Noah's Ark Scans This year, Dr Bakhtar utilised a more powerful radar system capable of reaching deeper underground structures and crevices.
 The team responsible for this year’s scans reported underground boundaries and structures, interpreting them as sediment-filled passageways, with five features forming a possible tunnel system.
 The reported tunnel system stretches roughly 46 metres and is about 4 metres high.
 Researchers also identified a thick underground layer with three distinct sublayers, consistent with the biblical account of three vessel decks.
 Radar scans that reportedly revealed a tunnel system through the midsection of the Durupinar Formation. Picture: Facebook, Noah's Ark Scans Noah’s Ark Scans founder Andrew Jones, who has researched the area for almost 30 years, told the Daily Mail that neither drilling in the formation nor radar surveys detected solid bedrock or limestone.
 “This destroys the theory that the site is a solid limestone block shaped into a boat by glaciers and weathering after coming down the mountainside, and it also refutes the theory that this is bedrock around which mud flowed to form the shape,” Mr Jones said.
 However, this does not prove that people built the formation.
 Mr Jones agrees that the findings do not definitively identify it as the biblical vessel itself.
 He called the scan results a “compelling new line of evidence”, not definitive proof.
 The Durupinar Formation was identified in 1959 by Turkish army captain Ilhan Durupinar, who noticed its boat-shaped outline in aerial photographs taken by NATO mapping missions about 29km (18 miles) from Mount Ararat.
